Let’s dive into Chapter 6: Predicting Violence: The Subtle Art of Pre-Incident Indicators.
You know, sometimes the most important warnings don’t come with blaring sirens or flashing lights. Instead, they show up as quiet, almost invisible signs—those little things you might notice in someone’s behavior or routine. We call these pre-incident indicators.
What’s wild is, most of us pick up on these signals way more often than we realize. Have you ever had that gut feeling, but couldn’t quite put your finger on why? Chances are, you were sensing one of these subtle cues.
Imagine this: There’s a manager in a busy office, juggling deadlines and back-to-back meetings. One employee, who’s usually pretty quiet, starts coming in early, staying late, and making little comments about being overlooked. At first, it just seems like normal job stress—nothing to worry about. But then, those offhand remarks get sharper, their mood swings become more unpredictable. The manager feels a little uneasy, but brushes it off, thinking, “I’m probably just overreacting.”
Later, when a confrontation blows up, all those early signs suddenly feel so obvious. Has that ever happened to you?
That’s exactly how pre-incident indicators work. They’re the small shifts—a change in someone’s routine, a comment that doesn’t quite fit, or a look that lingers just a little too long. Most of us are actually pretty good at noticing these things, but we talk ourselves out of it. Social norms, wanting to avoid drama, or just hoping things will get better—it’s easy to ignore what your instincts are trying to tell you.
Here’s something to remember: People who commit violence rarely act completely out of the blue. There are almost always clues. Maybe it’s an obsession, a sudden shift in attitude, or a growing fascination with weapons. Sometimes, it’s patterns of controlling behavior, or a history of pushing boundaries. Other times, you’ll see someone withdraw, lose interest in things they used to care about, or get fixated on a certain person or grievance.
For those who are willing to pay attention, these signals can be lifesaving. They’re a chance to step in, set some boundaries, or ask for help before things spiral out of control. The real challenge? Trusting what you see and feel, even when it’s uncomfortable. It’s so tempting to explain away a gut feeling as just being paranoid, or to hope that a rocky situation will sort itself out.
But time and again, people who’ve experienced violence later say, “The signs were there. I just didn’t want to believe them.”
You’ll see the same patterns pop up in families, at work, and all around your community. Maybe it’s a partner who suddenly gets possessive, a coworker who starts making veiled threats, or a neighbor whose behavior turns unpredictable. All of these are signs that something’s not quite right.
The real task is to notice, to take these signals seriously, and to act before things get worse.
It’s not about being fearful of everyone around you. It’s about being honest with yourself—really seeing what’s happening, not just what you hope is happening. Most violence can actually be predicted, if people are willing to look for the patterns.
The gift of fear isn’t just about sensing danger in the moment. It’s about recognizing the build-up—the patterns that lead there in the first place.
So, if you learn to notice and trust those pre-incident indicators, you’re not just protecting yourself. You’re looking out for the people around you too.
